/bandsintown.title: My Framer Site
h1: Local artists have to handle their own booking and promotion. A lack of connection to booking processes makes it difficult to connect with venues and other artists. Currently, Bandsintown artists reach out to other artists to build a bill primarily through Instagram and other social media platforms. Only after accommodating all participating musicians' schedules can they email a chosen venue to request to perform. Getting involved in the local music scene by performing at local venues allows them to connect with peers and generate more creative opportunities.

The role of the booking agent is to discover, review, and book artists to perform at their venue. Small venues, on the other hand, lack the resources of larger venues, including a dedicated booking agent. These small venues accommodate local music scenes, serving as important spaces for artists to advance their careers. Their value as social hubs and niche spaces of cultural production become an important ‘stepping stone’ for building musicians’ careers.
Foster and boost engagement among current members while attracting more musicians and venues to Bandsintown.

Foster and boost engagement among current members while attracting more musicians and venues to Bandsintown.Opportunity to showcase a broader, more diverse lineup of concerts while bringing visibility to local events for its audience.
Opportunity to showcase a broader, more diverse lineup of concerts while bringing visibility to local events for its audience.

Optimized organization of concerts removes the stress of planning, allowing artists to focus more on preparing their music. Eliminating the hassle of crafting perfect emails for every pitch by managing all outreach and proposals directly through the platform means more efficient and direct communication.
Providing a streamlined booking process can foster and boost

engagement among current members while attracting more musicians and venues to Bandsintown. By catering to smaller artist and venues, Bandsintown can showcase a broader, more diverse lineup of concerts while bringing visibility to local events.

Discover, connect, and stay up to date with others in your local music scene. 'Tune in' to fellow artists and venues to keep track of upcoming shows, see who's attending, and create more opportunities to connect and collaborate.

Venues make informed booking decisions by viewing artist booking requests. All necessary information is aggregated in one place, including music samples, performance videos, and scheduling information.

A guided, step-by-step booking process designed for clarity and accessibility. Artists can discover and invite collaborators, while clear button states distinguish pending invitations from accepted requests as they build their bill.
FRAMING, INITIAL DESIGN SOLUTION, & MOVING TO MOBILE

Our initial design solution focused on gamifying the experience by allowing artists and venues to “match” with one another based on their needs and musical styles. This would make it easier for artists to discover suitable venues and for venues to find artists who fit their space. However, after several rounds of class critiques, we realized that this approach did not truly address the problem of finding and connecting with venues. Instead, it functioned more like a curated list of suggested artists and venues, with the “matching” mechanic adding novelty without meaningfully improving the process.We ultimately pivoted toward a “Tune In” function that more closely follows an interaction model users are already familiar with: social media. Rather than creating an entirely new matching system, the feature would allow artists, venues, and audiences to discover and follow one another while keeping relevant information curated within a single platform. As Bandsintown is already an established platform, this intervention could also integrate naturally into its existing ecosystem rather than functioning as a separate service. We further structured the experience into clear steps with calendar integration, making it more than simply a messaging tool as our initial concept would have been. Although the idea of matching artists and venues based on musical styles and preferences was interesting, we ultimately felt that our final approach was better aligned with our stated problem and provided a more effective solution.

Another challenge we ran into centred on how we presented and communicated the design problem. We struggled to convince our audience that the problem we had identified was significant enough to warrant intervention. In early weeks, feedback made it clear that our proposed solution lacked excitement, while critics were also unconvinced that the problem itself was an issue that genuinely needed to be addressed.

However, during office hours, we received feedback that our actual reasoning was clear when explained conversationally. This made us realize that the issue was not necessarily with our justification, but with how effectively we communicated it through our presentation. To address this, we reframed our project to more clearly communicate the *why* behind our intervention and how it could benefit Bandsintown as a business while also supporting local artists and small venues. Given the nature of our proposed features, we were further encouraged to consider a mobile platform, which would provide users with more portable and accessible communication while aligning with a platform they are already accustomed to using.

This project pushed me to develop a deeper understanding of experience design through both research and application. Its structured process of constant, weekly presentations and critiques encouraged me to continuously iterate and defend design decisions. Rather than simply presenting a solution, I learned not only the importance of building a strong rationale behind each design choice but also communicating and justifying those ideas clearly to an audience.As a team project with a substantial workload, I learned to divide responsibilities effectively while maintaining a shared direction. Working independently and then reconvening to share research, readings, and design work required us to organize our thoughts, identify the most valuable insights, and then determine what should inform our next steps. Because the research phases played such a major role in shaping our project, it taught me that good design is not just about developing a solution, but also about understanding where a potential design lives and why it is needed.

Bandsintown Amplify is a live music booking and networking platform for artists and venues. By streamlining the processes required to create a live show, Bandsintown Amplify provides artists and venues an efficient and direct communication channel when booking that the existing Bandsintown does not. Large portions of reading and research were done beforehand to justify how and why this design helps a particular pain point amongst specific intended users in the local music community.
BANDSINTOWN AMPLIFY

Phase one of this project was heavily focused on reading about experience design. We learned through the lens of the intersection of business and design, examining how design operates within business. The reading touches on concepts such as a holistic experience whereby every touchpoint should be considered, through an iterative approach, to extend value to customers over time across all of the business's activities

Experience Design is, as the title of the Newbery and Farnham book suggests, a strategy and framework for integrating brand, experience and value. Using the customer journey diagram, we mapped the different stages of interaction for Philz Coffee and IKEA, looking into how each touchpoint contributes to the overall experience. This allowed us to practice identifying areas where value could be lost over time, as well as opportunities to strengthen engagement and re-engage customers beyond their initial interaction.

The next step included communicating this new learning and understanding of experience design through case studies that we selected as a team. We focused on analyzing the case studies to further decipher how brand value pillars should be implemented at each touchpoint to provide customers the long-term value during and after interaction. For each client, we found insights on potential problem spaces, evidence to prove the problem is real, and framing the issue to express "how might we…", "in order to…".

GMKGMK is a premium keycap manufacturer whose products are primarily discovered and purchased through third-party vendors and enthusiast communities. Research revealed that newcomers struggle to find reliable information on releases, purchasing options, and production updates, creating a high barrier to entry and contributing to counterfeit purchases. This led to the question: How might we connect newcomers and beginners to the necessary informational touchpoints needed to research, purchase, and stay updated on GMK keycaps in order to connect GMK directly with their customers, identify available purchase options, and provide production updates to reduce the high barrier of entry to GMK keycap designs?

THE ODD BUNCHThe Odd Bunch reduces food waste by selling surplus produce at lower prices. While this creates an affordable option for families facing rising grocery costs, research showed that meal planning and dietary flexibility remain challenges, particularly for households with limited time and picky eaters. This led to the question: How might we enable and support financially struggling families to incorporate diverse seasonal produce in order to promote healthy eating, making cooking and shopping efficient, while reducing food waste?

PEERSPACEPeerspace helps users book unique venues for events, but event planning extends far beyond securing a space. Research found that planners must independently source vendors, entertainment, and other services, while hosts are often expected to fill these gaps. This led to the question: How might we provide event planners holistic support during the event planning process (conception to execution) without burdening the venue hosts in order to efficiently craft a memorable and smooth event, leaving both event planners and hosts content with Peerspace?

Our final project ultimately shifted from the topics discussed above. As a group, we decided to focus on Bandsintown, exploring its online experience as a live music discovery platform. The following sections detail this direction and how we narrowed our focus.
-Interviewee 3, Local Vancouver Musician
-Interviewee 2, Local Vancouver Musician

Currently, the Bandsintown platform focuses on promotions catering mainly to artist-to-fan interactions, with less emphasis on the end process occurring before a show - how it is organized and scheduled. It loses points in terms of what goes into creating a bill and how that touchpoint is difficult for local artists and small venues who may not have the connections necessary.As opposed to Bandsintown's brand pillars, Songkick, a competitor service, prioritizes fan engagement by "always putting fans first." Functionality is also gated towards larger artists, with specific features lacked until an artist has a large enough following.
Pre-show and post-show touchpoints are equally—if not more—important for small artists and venues in organizing a successful live show, yet its never fully addressed on the platform.

While the overall progress remained steady, there were hurdles that highlighted the necessity of aligning Adobook more closely with its intended users. The app was developed with a focus on features like recipe addition and data collection, however, our initial user flow involved users manually inserting data through a fill-in-the-blank form. This led to an apparent challenge we faced during a class critique, where feedback indicated that this manual approach to data entry did not serve the app's target users well. Given that it's demographic includes seniors who may rely solely on hard copy recipes, Adobook needed to offer a more user-friendly solution for recipe entry.

To address this challenge, I proposed a feature enabling image scanning. This function would convert images into text, alleviating the need for manual data entry and thereby easing the usability for our target audience. Additionally, I proposed that the app should support audio recordings to further improved accessibility.

When the designs were completed, we conducted a pilot usability test with 9 participants (6 in-person & 3 online) to further refine our design and enhance the app's user interface experience. Including a Filipino family of three, the participants who were gathered for this usability test belonged to our user domain.

Participants were tasked with completing a series of interactions correlating to the main features of our prototype. After completing these tasks, users were asked to reflect on and answer questions relating to their experience. I assumed the role of observer and note-taker in this test, documenting events and feedback.

Below is a summarized overview of the test results, along with the issues I pinpointed during the session. While participants were very particular in their assessment of the interface design, this experience brought Adobook to a higher level of fidelity. I found the session highly informative, shedding light on users' perspectives and insights throughout the process.

Adobook turned out to be a well-researched project designed with its target users in mind. Researching a specific demographic helps guide a project in the right direction by providing a clearer understanding of the needs, preferences, and expectations of its intended audience. This ensures that the app is designed to address the needs of real users rather than relying solely on the assumptions of its designers. I learned the importance of conducting user testing, as feedback from intended users can reveal valuable insights and potential improvements that designers might otherwise overlook.

Through this project, I gained experience in task allocation and consistent scheduling, including regular check-ins with team members. By holding each other accountable and sharing constructive feedback, we were able to make steady progress while tools like a style guide also helped us maintain consistency throughout our work.

back

Adobook is a digital recipe book designed as an interactive mobile app allowing users to easily store, organize, and access their personal recipes. Created with accessibility in mind, it supports features like image scanning to convert handwritten or printed recipes into text, reducing the need for manual input. The app focuses on simplicity and inclusivity, making it especially suitable for users of all ages, including seniors.
Adobook hopes to keep Filipino traditions alive and preserve culture through food and community.

The purpose of this project was to create an interactive system. The team's first step included determining a target audience which we eventually narrowed down to a specific domain of people in which we could make a significant impact. This involved understanding their objectives, routines, potential growth areas, and obstacles. By focusing our scope on imigrant Filipino familes and interviewing them, I crafted one of three personas to guide the subsequent brainstorming sessions effectively.

Given the app's ethos, which emphasizes fostering a sense of family and serving as a portal for passing down recipes through generations, it was crucial to maintain a strong focus on Family. To achieve this, I developed a persona named Ashley Garcia, representing one of our primary audience segments. Ashley's persona details her relationship with her grandma and her characteristics, including pain points, goals, and motivations, ensuring our app resonates deeply with users like her.

During the brainstorming phase, we explored three potential directions for the project: a Recipe Translator, an Online Recipe-Sharing System, and a Digital Recipe Book. Following a constructive critique session, it was decided that the Digital Recipe Book held the most promise and aligned best with our goals.Like most design processes, I began by sketching out various concepts to generate ideas and visualize possibilities. Although each team member contributed their own designs, the final concept closely resembled my initial sketches. I subsequently transitioned these ideas into an initial Figma design, where we collaborated as a team to integrate everyone's input and refine the design.

A style guide was created to give each team member the freedom to design while working within the predetermined brand guidelines. This provided creative flexibility while ensuring that everyone’s work remained cohesive and consistent with the overall visual identity.

As we moved into the design phase, all team members collaborated to identify and develop the essential features of Adobook. With our end-users in mind, the team selected several key features, including viewing recipes, scanning or manually entering recipes, and translating recipes into different languages. Other aspects we also considered were the app’s layout and usability, focusing on a simple design with large, accessible buttons to make navigation easier for seniors.

/banditexpress.title: My Framer Site
h1: Jalene P (artist, game designer)Alicia L (programmer, game designer)
DIFFERENT TRAIN CAR SPRITES I HAD TO DESIGN AND ILLUSTRATE

A major iteration emerged during the “greenlight” review in week 3, when we received feedback that the game lacked a unique core mechanic. At that stage, the gameplay relied on fairly standard mechanics such as player shooting, platforming, and evading NPCs. Because the train itself did not meaningfully influence gameplay, playtests suggested that the experience was lacking and felt bland rather than exciting and unique as we had proposed. To tackle this challenge, we explored several ideas before settling on the train tilt mechanic.

Comments from participants indicated that the objective within each train car was unclear and that some mechanics were either not easily accessible or unnecessary to players. In response, we updated the functional flowboard to introduce individual tutorials for each mechanic at the start of the game and restructured gameplay so that destroying boxes became a primary mode of play. Part of solving this issue also involved redesigning the puzzles and adjusting breadcrumbing within a train car for a clearer objective.

In Week 9, feedback highlighted a lack of visual elements, which caused the game to fall short on personality when compared to our initial concept proposal. In response, between Weeks 9 and 12, I made the decision to fully revamp the art direction by adopting a pixel art style. This shift to more vibrant colors and style allowed for faster iteration on visual assets and, more importantly, better supported the sense of humour we were aiming for. Ultimately, the change successfully better defined the game’s fun narrative and intended humorous gameplay experience.

The development of Bandit Express was an iterative and collaborative process that evolved significantly from its initial concept. Early stages focused on ideation and defining the core direction of the game, with the team exploring multiple concepts before settling on a stealth-puzzle experience set on a moving train. As development progressed, consistent playtesting and critique sessions drove key primary mechanic decisions, including the shift away from combat towards environmental puzzle-solving and stealth. Timely critique sessions, technical milestones, and play tests allowed the team to refine core systems like player and NPC movement, train rotation, puzzle designs, and onboarding through narrative.

A key part of my contribution was deciding to revise the game’s visual direction. While early visuals established the initial world and characters, the later shift to a pixel art style and brighter color pallete brought stronger cohesion between the narrative and overall presentation. Although this required recreating all assets, the change better matched the game’s playful, light-hearted tone. The visual style also aligned more effectively with the game’s humour and intentionally “stupid protagonist” story, while improving gameplay clarity by making interactive elements and enemy states easier to recognize.

Overall, the project highlighted how interconnected all aspects of game development are. Solid core mechanics were essential before meaningful level and art polishing could occur, and feedback from playtesting continuously shaped both design and presentation. The process required constant iteration and clear communication within a small team, which ultimately led to a polished final game we are proud of. Seeing the project earn first place at the end-of-term showcase, where industry professionals played and evaluated each game, was a rewarding validation of our efforts.
h2: for detailed week by week blog
p: back to top
back

You're a fox cop so spectacularly bad at your job that when a train gets hijacked by raccoons, someone decides you're the best person to send in. With minimal help, your mission is to sneak through a train full of trash pandas and somehow reclaim the locomotive before they make off with the railway.

Bandit Express is a 2D third-person action-puzzle game. Progressing car by car, the game blends stealth, puzzle solving, physics-based challenges, and humour as players work their way toward a final showdown with the boss raccoon.

In the first week, our team explored a variety of game concepts before settling on our final direction. Initial brainstorming included an adventure game centred around a mischievous black cat that brings bad luck to the player, requiring them to outsmart the cat and uncover its motives through environmental storytelling and shadow-based mechanics. We also considered narrative-driven concepts such as a bartender simulator, where players could influence relationships through the drinks they served, and a similar flower shop concept involving listening to customer conversations and recommending flowers to play either cupid or devil.

As we explored branching narratives and endings, concerns about its complexity and feasibility led us to pivot. Early concepts of our final direction included playing as a passenger solving a mystery or as a train staff member managing passenger satisfaction. I later proposed shifting the focus to fighting through the train to reclaim the locomotive from an antagonist. Through further team iteration, this eventually evolved into our refined game proposal.
figma ideation board

Following a greenlight review in week 3, the team refined Bandit Express into a puzzle and stealth-focused experience. Combat was removed in favour of environmental problem-solving based on a water gun that destroys cardboard boxes, which also function as platforms. Following feedback during this phase, we introduced a unique train-tilting mechanic, where train cars incline or decline as it travels over hills to create more dynamic puzzles.

Alicia focused on designing the opening levels to introduce the core mechanics and narrative, while I focused on later puzzles that built on previously learned mechanics to increase complexity gradually. To help balance progression, I labelled the mechanics used in each level to track puzzle difficulty. Around this time, I also developed the game's narrative ending.

Alongside gameplay development, we produced a Game Design Document (GDD) outlining the core mechanics, and gameplay modes. To include artistic direction in the GDD, I additionally began sketching to explore character designs and visual styles that best captured the game's playful tone.
Our proposal in a nutshell: A gang of raccoons steals a train. The solution? Send in one very unqualified fox with a personal water gun.
Involves strategy to avoid raccoons and utilize objects around the player and their water gun
Collect coins, using them to successfully evade, then stun racoons
Solve puzzles to make their way through train cars towards the locomotive
Collect coins, using them to successfully evade then stun racoons

This flowboard was created during the early ideation stages of the project and reflects an initial direction. As development progressed, various mechanics and gameplay elements were added, removed, or revised.

By Week 5, we had developed our first playable prototype consisting of two train cars that tested the game's core systems including player movement, shooting, raccoon patrol and chase, box destruction, and train tilting. We also implemented higher-fidelity art assets with basic idle and walking animations. Through three playtesting sessions, we identified issues with unclear objectives and player movement, prompting us to refine our game's flowboard and prioritize smoother platforming. Improvements in the raccoons movements such as the coin-luring mechanics and other animations also had to be made.Despite this progress, the visuals were not at a stage that I was content with. Seeing all the assets together in-game and as a scene made it clear that the art direction wasn't aligning with the vision I had originally imagined. This realization highlighted the need for a stronger visual identity which ultimately led to a complete shift in the game's art style and color palette.

During the alpha milestone, my primary focus was designing and implementing the coin-luring mechanic, which was priority given where we stood in the timeline. It was important that players could collect, carry, and drop coins to lure raccoons away from key areas and progress through the game. By using a finite-state machine, I could ensure the mechanics felt intuitive and responsive enough when integrated into the puzzle design.

Alongside this, I continued creating animations for walking and charmed raccoon states that visually communicated when raccoons were attracted to nearby coins. These additions were necessary in strengthening player feedback and made the mechanic feel more engaging during gameplay.

Following the alpha code presentation, our team continued to polish both the art and code. Cardboard friction dynamics (so boxes slide differently depending on train tilt) were improved, and automatic doors were implemented to open when the train stabilizes. We also added multiple train rotation states and started looping background art to simulate motion. Additional raccoon animations and animated cutscenes were also prepared for the beta code. Moving forward, we planned to fix issues with jump consistency pertaining to collision detection during train rotation and while hitting door triggers.
Shortly after beginning the cutscene animations, I decided to change the art style and entire visual direction.

By the beta build, substantial progress was made in both art and gameplay systems. Final elements such as player checkpoints, a restart feature, a dialogue radio tutorial system (mechanics onboarding), and cutscene transitions were added to complete the game as much as possible before the deadline. In addition to asset creation, I pushed level design a bit further especially in later parts of the game. On the code side, I was able to fix small bugs such as player jumping issues and incorrect raccoon movement. In repsonse to class feedback about repetitive train cars, I also designed more unique train car sprites at each level for visual variety and interest.
